summary: Via Virtus is a web map for planning surface traverses from a candidate crew base at Arcadia Planitia, Mars (39.8°N, 157.9°W), where orbital radar indicates shallow ground ice. We reprojected NASA and ESA orbital data onto a 200 m grid covering 227 × 154 km around the base: HRSC–MOLA elevation, a CTX terrain model, THEMIS thermal imagery and Viking color imagery. For five scientific sites, the app computes the optimal route from the base, avoiding slopes the rover or astronaut cannot climb, and answers the key survival question: can we get there and back? For an electric rover, it compares the battery needed for the round trip against a 20% reserve. The ice-mining site needs 61 of 96 kWh, while the megaripple field, 118 km away, is one-way only. On foot, it calculates oxygen, the number of 8-hour EVAs, and metabolic and body-heat alerts from the astronaut’s mass, suit and pace. On Mars, energy and oxygen limit how far a crew can go. This tool turns open orbital data into clear go/no-go decisions before anyone leaves the base.
details:
What it does
Via Virtus is a map for planning trips on Mars. It starts at a candidate base in Arcadia Planitia, where there is ice just below the surface, and for each of five science sites it answers one question: can the crew get there and back? Pick a site and choose rover or on foot. The app draws the best route and tells you what the trip will cost.

How it works
We took NASA and ESA orbital data and put it on a single 200 m map around the base: elevation, terrain detail, thermal and color images. From the elevation we found the safest paths, avoiding slopes that are too steep. For the rover, the app calculates how much battery the trip uses and keeps 20% in reserve. AP-9, the ice site, is a safe round trip. The megaripple field, 118 km away, is one-way only. On foot, it calculates oxygen, how many 8-hour EVAs are needed, and when the astronaut’s body would overheat.










Why it matters
On Mars, distance isn’t the real limit. Energy and oxygen are. Via Virtus turns raw orbital data into a clear go or no-go decision before anyone leaves the base. It also shows which unknowns matter most. The biggest one is how hard it is to roll over Martian soil, so that is the first thing a real mission should measure.






How we built it
We used Python to process the data and JavaScript with Leaflet for the map. More than 300 automated tests keep the numbers consistent, and the site is hosted on GitHub Pages. It runs in any browser with nothing to install. We wrote the code with help from AI coding agents and checked every result with tests.

What makes it different
It plans for both machines and people. Every assumption is listed with its source, and the app is honest about its limits. A route is only useful if you know you can come back.
dataRefs: Mars MGS MOLA – MEX HRSC Blended DEM Global 200m v2 (elevation, slope, roughness, routes)
Mars MGS MOLA DEM 463m (backup elevation source)
MRO CTX Controlled DTMs and Orthoimages, USGS STAC (detail layer near the base)
Mars Odyssey THEMIS Day IR Global Mosaic 100m v12 (thermal layer)
HiRISE ESP_052424_2200 / ESP_052490_2200, Arcadia Planitia candidate landing site (base site context)
NASA Mars Trek (visual check of site positions)
NASA NTRS: PLSS design rules, 8-hour EVA (suit and EVA limits)
NASA NTRS: Mars suit mass and VO₂-to-energy equation, ICES 2026
NASA NTRS: Astronaut and rover traverse limits (LPSC 2026)
projectRefs: ESA Mars Express HRSC (part of the blended DEM, with DLR and FU Berlin)
Tesla Model S official specifications (reference vehicle for the rover model)
Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking on slopes
Looney et al. 2018, Metabolic costs of load carriage over complex terrain
